q: Some pearlfish find shelter by entering which living animal through its anus?

q: Why can a sabretooth blenny’s resemblance to a cleaner wrasse be bad news for larger fish?
a: It bites flesh instead of cleaning
d: The mimic’s appearance and movements let it approach fish expecting parasite removal.
choices: It bites flesh instead of cleaning
It steals food from their mouths
It attacks the real cleaner fish
It chases them from feeding territory
s: University of Hawai‘i · Cleaners and mimics
evidence: Account describes blenny mimicry of cleaner wrasse and bites to client tissue.

q: Researchers photographed an albatross doing what helpful service for an ocean sunfish?
d: The fish appeared to present themselves sideways while the birds picked attached parasites.
choices: Pulling seaweed out of its mouth
Turning it upright after a dive
s: Abe and colleagues · Sunfish and albatross cleaning
evidence: Primary observation photographed a Laysan albatross taking and eating a Pennella parasite from a sunfish.

q: A jewel wasp delivers a precisely aimed sting to which part of a cockroach to suppress its urge to escape?
d: The roach can still move, but its spontaneous escape behavior is greatly reduced.
s: Gal and colleagues · Jewel wasp stinger senses
evidence: Primary experiments support mechanical sensing of brain tissue and targeted venom delivery.

q: In a mirror experiment, what did marked cleaner wrasses do after seeing a brown spot on their own throats?
a: Scrape their throats on the substrate
d: The observed response depended on the mirror and a parasite-like mark. What it demonstrates about self-awareness remains debated.
choices: Scrape their throats on the substrate
Peck at the mirror’s brown spot
Display their fins at the reflection
Try to feed the reflected fish
s: Kohda and colleagues · Cleaner-fish mirror experiments
evidence: Study reports throat scraping with brown marks and mirrors; controls without mirrors or differently colored marks did not show the same response.

q: After developing inside a cricket or another insect, where does an adult horsehair worm usually need to emerge to reproduce?
d: The long, thin parasite’s adult reproductive stage is aquatic.
s: University of Florida IFAS · Horsehair worms
evidence: Extension account describes parasitic immature stages and free-living aquatic adults; avoids overstating host mind-control.

q: The parasite Leucochloridium creates conspicuous pulsating swellings in which parts of an infected snail?
d: Colorful broodsacs occupy the tentacles. Their resemblance to caterpillars may attract the birds needed for the parasite’s life cycle.
s: Nakao and colleagues · Leucochloridium in Japan
evidence: Primary abstract describes pulsating colorful broodsacs within snail eyestalks; caterpillar mimicry is qualified as apparent.

q: A stoplight loosejaw’s red-light vision is aided by a derivative of which familiar plant pigment?
d: The unusual visual sensitizer reaches the fish through its food chain.
s: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution · Stoplight loosejaw
evidence: WHOI links red perception to chlorophyll-related pigments acquired through copepod prey.

q: Venezuela’s Casiquiare provides a natural river link between the Orinoco and which other enormous drainage basin?
d: It branches from the Orinoco and joins the Rio Negro, carrying water into the Amazon system.
s: NASA Earth Observatory · Rivers taking weird turns
evidence: NASA describes Casiquiare as both Orinoco distributary and Amazon tributary.

q: What has been smoldering underground at Australia’s Burning Mountain?
d: The heat comes from slow combustion below the sandstone, not an active volcano.
s: NSW National Parks · Burning Mountain
evidence: Park authority identifies a naturally burning underground coal seam.

q: What powers the dramatic Horizontal Falls in Western Australia’s Talbot Bay?
d: Restricted passages hold back the tidal flow, producing powerful differences in water level.
choices: River floods spilling over sea cliffs
s: Western Australia fisheries · Talbot Bay
evidence: Official fact sheet attributes horizontal waterfall effect to tidal buildup behind narrow rock gaps.

q: Some New Guinea skinks have bright green blood because they accumulate which substance?
d: High concentrations of biliverdin overwhelm the red appearance of their blood cells.
s: Austin and Jessing · Green-blood pigmentation in lizards
evidence: Primary paper identifies unusually high plasma biliverdin concentrations in Prasinohaema.

q: A threatened Iberian newt can push what through its own skin as a defensive weapon?
d: The sharp bones pierce the skin and encounter toxic secretions that deter a biting predator.
s: Freshwater Biology · Iberian newt rib defense
evidence: Paper describes protractile ribs emerging through toxin-producing skin warts.

q: Which members of a weaver-ant colony supply the silk used to join leaves into nests?
d: Their silk is put into communal construction instead of individual cocoons.
s: Hölldobler and Wilson · Weaver-ant larval silk
evidence: Primary abstract identifies final-instar Oecophylla longinoda larvae as nest-silk producers.

q: Some desert ants turn special workers into what kind of living colony equipment?
d: Their abdomens swell with liquid food that can later be shared with nestmates.
s: Smithsonian Natural History · Honeypot-ant exhibit
evidence: Museum describes replete workers as living food-storage containers.

q: A sea otter collecting several prey items on one dive can stash them in what built-in storage space?
d: The skin fold works like a pocket, holding food until the otter returns to the surface.
s: US Fish and Wildlife Service · Southern sea otter
evidence: Official account identifies loose armpit skin as a pocket storing multiple prey from a dive.

q: During floods, fire ants can survive by assembling what from their own bodies?
d: Interlocking ants form a water-repellent structure that keeps the colony afloat.
s: Georgia Tech Ant Lab · Ant raft
evidence: Lab describes fire ants linking into water-repellent rafts on rising water.

q: The tiger moth Bertholdia trigona can thwart hunting bats by producing rapid sounds that do what?
d: Ultrasonic clicks interfere with the bats’ use of returning echoes.
choices: Signal that the moth tastes unpleasant
Startle them with a low-frequency thump
s: Corcoran and colleagues · Tiger-moth sonar jamming
evidence: Primary study tests and supports sonar jamming by the specified moth.

q: A luna moth’s trailing hindwing tails help it escape bats by doing what?
a: Diverting attacks away from its body
d: Moving tails create misleading acoustic targets; a bat may grab expendable wing material.
choices: Diverting attacks away from its body
Advertising its sex to potential mates
Making the entire moth echo less strongly
s: Florida Museum · Luna moth tail defense
evidence: Researchers describe spinning hindtails diverting sonar-guided attacks.

q: What effect can the tiny scales of some moth wings have on a hunting bat’s returning echoes?
d: Reducing reflected bat calls makes the moth harder to detect by echolocation.
choices: Split them into widely separated false targets
Shift them into audible human frequencies
Reflect them back with an added delay
s: University of Bristol · Moth acoustic camouflage
evidence: Research found ultrasound-absorptive properties in the thin scale layer.

q: A beetle seeking freshly burned wood for breeding has specialized pit organs that can detect what signal from a fire?
d: Melanophila beetles have infrared-sensitive organs. This unusual heat detection helps them locate forest fires and the breeding habitat left behind.
s: Evans and colleagues · Melanophila infrared pit organs
evidence: Primary abstract describes detection of fire-emitted infrared by paired thoracic pit organs.

q: Besides using lungs, the Mary River turtle can extract oxygen through which unlikely body region?
d: Specialized surfaces in this rear chamber take up oxygen from water.
s: Australian Museum · Mary River turtle
evidence: Museum describes cloacal oxygen uptake in Mary and Fitzroy river turtles.

q: What does a garden snail’s “love dart” deliver that can improve the shooter’s reproductive success?
d: Experiments found the gland secretion increased paternity by affecting the mate’s reproductive system.
s: Chase and Blanchard · Snail love darts
evidence: Primary experiment found mucus injections increased paternity relative to saline controls.

q: Researchers filmed southern resident killer whales making mutual grooming tools from what?
d: They cut pieces of stalk and rolled them between their bodies; skin care and social bonding are proposed benefits.
s: University of Exeter · Killer-whale grooming tools
evidence: Drone observations show whales manufacturing and using kelp stalk pieces for allogrooming.

q: Some humpback whales corral fish before lunging upward by blowing what around them?
d: The moving bubble barrier concentrates prey into a smaller feeding area.
s: NOAA Fisheries · Humpback whale
evidence: NOAA describes prey pushed upward within circular bubble nets.

q: A walrus can remove a clam’s soft body from its shell mainly by using what?
d: Its mouth and tongue create a powerful pressure difference.
choices: A cutting edge on its tongue
s: Smithsonian Ocean · Pinnipeds
evidence: Museum describes efficient suction feeding on clam flesh.

q: What surprisingly mammal-like bathroom performance did researchers film in tiny cicadas?
d: The studied cicadas expelled a continuous liquid stream. Their watery diet creates a large fluid load, making this efficient despite their small size.
s: Georgia Tech — Cicadas’ Unique Urination
evidence: Researchers observed cicadas jetting urine instead of droplets; their liquid diet makes jetting energetically useful.

q: What lets a harbor seal follow a fish’s lingering trail even in murky water?
d: The whiskers detect water movements left behind by a swimming fish.
s: MIT Towing Tank · Seal whiskers
evidence: Research account describes whisker detection of hydrodynamic wakes.

q: Which Australian marsupial has individually distinctive fingerprints with patterns similar to ours?
d: Its ridged fingertips evolved in a lineage far removed from humans and apes.
s: Henneberg and colleagues · Koala fingerprint homoplasy
evidence: Primary article compares fingertip dermatoglyphic ridges in koalas and humans; avoids crime-scene confusion myth.

q: How does a male bedbug deliver sperm during its unusual form of mating?
d: The process is called traumatic insemination.
choices: Attaching a packet to her wings
s: Reinhardt and colleagues · Traumatic insemination
evidence: Primary abstract describes needle-like intromittent organ puncturing female cuticle.

q: Brain recordings showed northern elephant seals doing what during some deep-ocean dives?
d: During REM sleep, the seals could turn belly-up and drift in descending spirals. Their naps took place while they held their breath far below the surface.
choices: Sleeping while circling at one depth
s: Scripps Institution of Oceanography — Elephant Seal Sleep
evidence: Brain monitoring linked REM sleep paralysis to upside-down downward sleep spirals during deep dives.

q: What does a bullethead parrotfish produce at night that experiments found works like a mosquito net?
d: The temporary covering reduces attacks by small blood-feeding crustacean parasites.
s: Grutter and colleagues · Fish mucous cocoons
evidence: Experiment found intact cocoons reduced gnathiid attacks compared with removed cocoons.

q: Certain Bornean ants defend their colony by rupturing their own bodies to release what onto an opponent?
d: The fatal release entangles the attacker in glue-like material.
s: Hoenigsberger and colleagues · Colobopsis gland chemistry
evidence: Paper describes minor workers rupturing the gaster and releasing sticky mandibular-gland contents.

q: Researchers studying two sea-slug species saw detached heads regenerate what?
d: The surviving heads rebuilt the missing body. The discarded bodies did not grow new heads, making the recovery strikingly one-sided.
s: Mitoh and Yusa — Extreme autotomy and whole-body regeneration
evidence: Primary abstract reports head survival and whole-body regeneration including the heart; discarded bodies did not regenerate heads.

q: After leaving the ocean, some flying squid can keep accelerating through the air by doing what?
d: Photographs captured an airborne powered phase followed by gliding. Spread arms and fins provide lifting surfaces, which are folded for reentry.
choices: Paddling the air with their arms
Expelling a jet of swallowed air
s: Hokkaido University — Oceanic squid flight
evidence: Sequential photographs documented water jetting after launch, followed by gliding with spread arms and fins.

q: An American lobster releases urine through openings at which surprising location?
d: The paired outlets sit at the front of the animal. Water currents carry urine forward, and its chemical signals play a role in social encounters.
s: Breithaupt, Lindstrom and Atema — Lobster urine release
evidence: Primary paper introduction locates paired nephropores on ventral basal segments of second antennae; full text read in author-uploaded Academia copy.

q: The elongated tongue-supporting apparatus of a woodpecker follows which surprising route?
a: Around the outside of its skull
d: Long hyoid structures curve around the head and help operate the probing tongue. Their exact arrangement varies among woodpecker species.
choices: Around the outside of its skull
Along the inside of its spine
Across the front of its breastbone
s: Jung et al. — Woodpecker tongue and hyoid structure
evidence: Structural study describes elongated hyoid horns around the skull, with species-specific extensions toward nasal or orbital regions.

q: In an experiment using a jacket around a narwhal’s tusk, changes in which water property produced heart-rate responses?
d: High- and low-salt water passed over the tusk in separate tests. The responses supported a sensory pathway between the exposed tooth and the animal’s nervous system.
s: Harvard Gazette — Secrets of the narwhal tusk
evidence: Tusk-jacket tests varied water salinity; Holter monitors recorded significant changes in heart rate.

q: Some ants can launch themselves out of a predator’s pit by striking the ground with which body parts?
d: Their rapid mandible closure supplies the impulse for an escape jump. Laboratory encounters showed that these jumps can help ants survive antlion attacks.
s: Duke University Patek Lab — Trap-jaw ant movement
evidence: Lab explains intentional mandible-powered escape jumps with head alignment before ground strike; linked predator experiments support escape value.

q: How can an antlion larva keep prey sliding toward the bottom of its sandy pit?
d: Sand tossing helps maintain steep, unstable slopes and can trigger slides that carry prey toward the waiting larva.
choices: Packing the slopes with smooth leaves
s: Büsse et al. — Sand-throwing in antlion larvae
evidence: Experiments and finite-element modeling found sand throwing maintains near-unstable slopes and resulting slides can relocate prey to the center.

q: An adult Turritopsis dohrnii jellyfish can reverse its development and return to which earlier stage?
d: Under stress, the swimming medusa can shrink into a cyst and develop into a polyp, which can produce new medusae. The ability does not protect it from being eaten.
s: Natural History Museum — Immortal jellyfish
evidence: Museum account describes stressed medusa becoming a cyst and then a new polyp; not literal invulnerability.

q: When researchers placed two injured Mnemiopsis comb jellies together, what surprising recovery could occur?
a: Their bodies fused and shared functions
d: The joined animals coordinated contractions, and food could pass through connected digestive channels. Researchers documented integration after injury in this species.
choices: Their bodies fused and shared functions
One consumed the other and regrew
Each formed a protective external capsule
Both divided into smaller separate animals
s: Jokura et al. — Rapid physiological integration of fused ctenophores
evidence: Primary abstract reports injured individuals fusing with integrated physiology and neurobehavior; MBL institutional account confirms shared digestive transport.

q: A great bowerbird arranges display objects in a size gradient that creates which visual effect for a visiting female?
d: Objects become larger farther from the viewing position, making their apparent sizes more uniform. Males restored the gradient after researchers reversed it.
s: Endler et al. — Great bowerbird forced perspective
evidence: Primary abstract documents increasing object size with distance, uniform visual angles, and restoration after experimental reversal.

q: In 1980, Louisiana’s Lake Peigneur began draining into what underground space after a drilling accident?
d: The expanding opening swallowed water and large surface objects. Salt dissolved as water rushed in, and a connecting canal reversed its flow to refill the lake.
s: University of Louisiana at Lafayette Archives — Lake Peigneur disaster
evidence: Archival institutional account documents lake draining into Diamond Crystal salt mine after drilling breach and canal flow reversal.

q: Which paired structures on a barn owl sit at different heights and help it pinpoint prey?
d: The offset openings work with the owl’s sound-funneling facial feathers to help locate rustling prey.
s: Natural History Museum — Barn owl
evidence: Museum describes ears set at slightly different heights and heart-shaped face directing sounds for prey localization.

q: Where do acorn woodpeckers commonly pack thousands of nuts for later meals?
d: A communal storage tree becomes a granary, with nuts fitted into separate holes. Groups defend the stores and may also use wooden human structures.
choices: A single large hollow nest cavity
s: Cornell Lab of Ornithology — Acorn Woodpecker
evidence: Cornell describes thousands of acorns stored in individually drilled granary-tree holes and guarded by group members.

q: Newcastle researchers attached what miniature equipment to praying mantises to test how they judged prey distance?
d: Blue and green filters let the team present different images to the two eyes. Mantises struck at virtual prey when the images placed it within apparent reach.
s: Newcastle University — Mantis 3D-glasses research
evidence: Institutional research account describes blue-green glasses, virtual bug stimuli, and strikes at apparently reachable 3D targets.

q: A 2024 experiment shortened which animal’s dives by disrupting its ability to rebreathe an air bubble?
d: Water anoles repeatedly draw in air from a bubble over their nostrils. Lizards whose normal bubbles were impaired surfaced sooner than the controls.
s: Swierk — Rebreathing extends anole dive time
evidence: Primary experiment on Anolis aquaticus blocked normal bubble formation with emollient; rebreathing and dive duration declined. No established physical-gill claim.
